summary.text: Assuming the claimed formula, the shifted terms \(a_n+1\) follow the Fibonacci matrix recurrence; a finite computation of the initial residues and matrix exponentiation modulo \(p=195318521017\) show that \(p\mid a_{249580077006}\) and \(p\mid a_{249580077007}\). Their gcd is therefore greater than 1, so the defining gcd recurrence at index \(249580077008\) cannot equal \(1+a_{249580077007}+a_{249580077006}\), contradicting the assumed formula.

full_proof.text:
Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be the sequence defined by
\[
a_1=a_2=1,
\qquad
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n}\quad(n\geq3),
\qquad
g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We disprove the conjecture by showing that even its first asserted identity
\[
 a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\tag{1}
\]
cannot hold for every \(n\geq3775\). Consequently, the conjunction of (1) with the other two claimed formulas cannot hold for every such \(n\), either.

The proof uses the following integers:
\[
\begin{aligned}
p&=195318521017,\\
m&=249580073233,\\
k&=3774+m=249580077007,\\
N&=k+1=249580077008.
\end{aligned}
\]
No primality assertion about \(p\) is needed; all that matters is that \(p>1\).

We first record two finite modular calculations.

### 1. The initial residues

Direct iteration of the defining recurrence through index \(3774\) gives
\[
 a_{3774}+1\equiv 99768150822\pmod p,
 \qquad
 a_{3773}+1\equiv 77940394259\pmod p.\tag{2}
\]
For completeness, this finite calculation is performed entirely over the integers as follows. Start with the ordered pair \((u,v)=(1,1)=(a_1,a_2)\). For each \(j=3,4,\ldots,3774\), replace
\[
 (u,v)
 \quad\text{by}\quad
 \left(v,\ d+\frac{u+v}{d}\right),
 \qquad d=\gcd(u,v).
\]
At the end the pair is \((a_{3773},a_{3774})\). Euclidean gcd calculations and integer divisions in these 3772 steps give
\[
 a_{3773}\equiv77940394258\pmod p,
 \,\qquad
 a_{3774}\equiv99768150821\pmod p,
\]
which is (2). The divisions are exact because \(d\) divides both \(u\) and \(v\), hence divides \(u+v\).

### 2. A Fibonacci-matrix calculation

Work modulo \(p\), and put
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Repeated squaring gives
\[
M^m\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}
139205883321&21827756563\\
21827756563&117378126758
\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p.\tag{3}
\]
Here is a complete addition-chain certificate for (3). In each row, the four entries after the exponent \(e\) are the entries of \(M^e\), reduced to the interval \([0,p-1]\). From one row to the next, the new exponent is either \(2e\), in which case the displayed matrix is obtained by squaring the preceding matrix modulo \(p\), or \(2e+1\), in which case it is obtained by squaring and then multiplying by \(M\). Multiplying the final matrix in the table by the residue vector from (2) gives
\[
M^m

\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p.\tag{4}
\]
The two unreduced dot products, together with their Euclidean divisions by \(p\), are
\[
\begin{aligned}
139205883321\cdot99768150822
 +21827756563\cdot77940394259
 &=15589577514788957011679\\
 &=79816176334\,p+1,
\\[3pt]

 +117378126758\cdot77940394259
 &=11326212385784681827108\\
 &=57988419771\,p+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (4) by directly checkable integer arithmetic.

### 3. Consequence of the conjectured recurrence

Suppose, for contradiction, that all three conjectured identities hold for every \(n\geq3775\). We use only (1).

Set
\[
x_n=a_n+1.
\]
If (1) holds at \(n\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_n
 &=a_n+1\\
 &=2+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\\
 &=(a_{n-1}+1)+(a_{n-2}+1)\\
 &=x_{n-1}+x_{n-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus, for every \(n\geq3775\),
\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_n\\x_{n-1}\end{pmatrix}
=M\begin{pmatrix}x_{n-1}\\x_{n-2}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
By induction on \(t\geq0\), this yields
\[
\begin{pmatrix}x_{3774+t}\\x_{3773+t}\end{pmatrix}
=M^t\begin{pmatrix}x_{3774}\\x_{3773}\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{5}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(t=0\); multiplying by \(M\) and using the recurrence at index \(3775+t\) proves the step from \(t\) to \(t+1\).

Reduce (5) modulo \(p\) and take \(t=m\). Combining (2) and (4), and recalling that \(3774+m=k\), gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}a_k+1\\a_{k-1}+1\end{pmatrix}
\equiv
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}
\pmod p.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_k\equiv0\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{k-1}\equiv0\pmod p.\tag{6}
\]
In particular, \(p\) divides both consecutive terms \(a_k\) and \(a_{k-1}\).

Both of these terms are positive. For example, under the assumed identity (1), since \(k-1\geq3775\),
\[
a_{k-1}=1+a_{k-2}+a_{k-3}\geq1,
\]
and similarly \(a_k\geq1\). (Positivity also follows directly by induction from the defining recurrence.)

### 4. Failure at the next step

Let
\[
a=a_k,\qquad b=a_{k-1},\qquad g=\gcd(a,b).
\]
By (6), \(p\mid a\) and \(p\mid b\), hence
\[
p\mid g.
\]
Since \(p>1\) and \(g>0\), it follows that \(g\geq2\).

Because \(g\) is the gcd, write
\[
a=gA,
\qquad b=gB
\]
for positive integers \(A,B\). The actual defining recurrence at index
\(N=k+1\) gives
\[
a_N=g+\frac{a+b}{g}=g+A+B.\tag{7}
\]
On the other hand, the conjectured identity (1), applied at the same index \(N\), would give
\[
a_N=1+a+b=1+gA+gB.\tag{8}
\]
These two values cannot be equal. In fact, subtracting the right-hand side of (7) from the right-hand side of (8) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1+gA+gB)-(g+A+B)
 &= (g-1)(A+B-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(g-1\geq1\), while \(A,B\geq1\) implies \(A+B-1\geq1\). Hence this difference is strictly positive. Thus
\[
g+\frac{a+b}{g}\ne1+a+b,
\]
contradicting the assertion of (1) at \(N=249580077008\), which certainly satisfies \(N\geq3775\).

We have therefore shown that the identity \(a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\) cannot hold at every index \(n\geq3775\). Since the OEIS conjecture asserts this identity together with two additional identities at every such index, the full conjecture is false.
